255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An: The title riffs on The Godfather, but the godfather here is Friedrich Nietzsche, the nineteenth-century German philosopher long accused of inspiring Nazism. Hitler was photographed before Nietzsche's bust, Mussolini quoted "live dangerously," and Nietzsche's sister Elisabeth curated his legacy for the regime. The essays ask how that happened: whether his ideas of power and the Übermensch were genuinely proto-fascist or grotesquely distorted, what he really wrote about the Jews, and whether an author bears responsibility for being misread.
256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy -: Anthony Bourdain was the chef-turned-travel-writer whose books and shows, from Kitchen Confidential to Parts Unknown, took him eating everything from street noodles to cobra hearts around the world until his death in 2018. He emerges here as a philosopher in his own right: essays treat his Socratic humility and risk-taking as gateways to questions about taste and snobbery, why disgusting foods can be delicious, the ethics of culinary tourism in poor countries, authenticity, freedom, friendship, and Camus's question of whether life is worth living.
258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Kn: South Park is the Comedy Central cartoon that since 1997 has sent four foul-mouthed Colorado boys through absurd, deliberately offensive stories skewering everything from Scientology to political correctness. The essays treat the show as a modern Socratic gadfly: the Chewbacca Defense becomes a lesson in logic, Stan's debunking of psychics and religions embodies the ethics of belief, and Cartman's casual cruelty illustrates the banality of evil. Detours through The Matrix and Battlestar Galactica widen the questions of skepticism, faith, and what we owe the truth.
259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island H: Lost was the ABC drama (2004-2010) about the survivors of a plane crash stranded on a mysterious island, famous for flashbacks, time travel, and a tangle of unresolved mysteries. The island setting is a philosophical thought experiment: cut off from everything familiar, the characters must ask why they are there and whether their lives matter. Essays work through the logic of its time travel, whether foreknowledge cancels free will, justice among castaways rationing scarce medicine, and what fixed character means when circumstances keep changing.
260 - The Daily Show and Philosophy - Mo: The Daily Show, under Jon Stewart from 1999 to 2015, was Comedy Central's "fake news" program that satirized cable news and politics so sharply it became a serious force in American public life. That paradox is the book's engine: how can comedy be fake and still tell the truth? Essays ask whether satire informs or merely amuses, whether jokes can substitute for reasoned citizenship, what Stewart's Crossfire and Cramer interviews accomplished, and whether television itself, as Neil Postman feared, makes real discourse impossible.
261 - Philosophy in The Twilight Zone: The Twilight Zone was Rod Serling's anthology series (1959-1964), famous for twist endings that turned ordinary situations — a time-obsessed bookworm, a robot companion, a too-friendly stranger — into unsettling moral puzzles. That is exactly the material of philosophy. Essays examine the logic of time travel across episodes, why Serling's camera and mirror imagery feels uncanny, whether a man can truly love a robot, what faces tell us about trust and deception, and how the show dramatizes our self-delusion about love, justice, and second chances.
262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the: Dr. Seuss — the pen name of Theodor Geisel — wrote the rhyming children's books generations know by heart: Horton, the Grinch, the Sneetches, the Lorax. Their simple plots turn out to carry real philosophical weight. Essays read Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' examined life, the Sneetches through Marx on alienation and consumption, Yertle the Turtle through the social contract, and the Lorax through business and environmental ethics, while Green Eggs and Ham becomes a primer on how stubborn belief can change.
263 - Stephen King and Philosophy: Stephen King is America's most famous horror writer, author of Carrie, The Shining, Pet Sematary, and the eight-volume Dark Tower saga. The essays argue his horror is philosophy by other means: Desperation stages the problem of evil, Carrie becomes a study of female subjectivity through Simone de Beauvoir, Pet Sematary weighs the transhumanist dream of abolishing death, and Roland's endless quest enacts Nietzsche's eternal recurrence. King's monsters force readers to confront finitude, suffering, and the values they actually live by.
264 - Jane Austen and Philosophy: Jane Austen published six novels in the early nineteenth century — Pride and Prejudice, Emma, Persuasion among them — whose marriage plots have made her beloved for two centuries. The essays argue she is an "accidental philosopher": her heroines' struggle to be believed raises epistemic injustice; her ideal marriages match Aristotle's complete friendship; her courtship clashes invite Nietzsche on happiness; and Charlotte Lucas's pragmatic match shows love never escapes economics. Beneath the romance lies a sharp analysis of women's vulnerability, virtue, and self-knowledge.
265 - Mark Twain and Philosophy: Mark Twain, the great American humorist behind Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, was also a serious moral thinker hiding behind the jokes. The essays center on Huck's decision not to turn in the escaped slave Jim: his conscience told him he was sinning, his sympathy told him otherwise, and philosophers have argued for decades about what that shows. Other essays take up Twain's dark late writings on religion and the problem of evil, the ethics of lying, and his case against human exceptionalism.
